conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ll follow up with hepatology and rheumatology. They’ll guide next steps, possibly more imaging or a biopsy when it’s safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has improved. You’ve been off IV fluids since yesterday. How’s your appetite?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had oatmeal this morning and kept it down. Still feel a bit full in the upper belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild tenderness in the RUQ and epigastrium is still there, but no signs of obstruction on imaging. We’ll keep your furosemide at your home dose now that you’re eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’ve been worried about that too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart is stable. Troponins were negative, so no heart attack. EKG shows your usual pattern. We’re continuing your beta-blocker and aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held glyburide while you weren’t eating. You’re on sliding scale insulin. Now that you’re back on food, we’re restarting glyburide at a lower dose—5 mg twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your stool cultures came back negative. No infection found. We’re finishing up the antibiotics today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was just a stomach bug?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly, yes. But your liver issues and inflammation are separate. We’re treating the infection, but the bigger picture needs outpatient follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take warfarin 7.5 mg daily. Get your INR checked on the scheduled day and call the anticoagulation clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for nausea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have Compazine and Zofran. Take one before meals if you feel nauseous. Also, monitor your weight—call if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting. Use your walker as needed. Keep all your follow-up appointments—especially with liver and rheumatology.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. You’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with instructions. Take your meds as listed, especially warfarin and the nausea tablets as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with the specialists. Any red flags to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If nausea or diarrhea returns, or if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or severe belly pain, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And nosebleeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If it doesn’t stop in 10 minutes or happens often, let us know. But occasional minor bleeding is okay for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. You’re alert, vitals are stable, and you’ve tolerated food well. All set to go home with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take these prescriptions. The home health nurse will visit to check your INR and help with meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels. Call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in last night with weakness and low blood counts. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been feeling weak and dizzy for a few days. I’ve also had nosebleeds—almost every day—and my urine has been pink with clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how long has that been happening?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About four days. The nosebleeds were constant at first, but they’ve slowed. I haven’t had one since yesterday, just two small episodes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. Your blood work shows your hemoglobin dropped from 35 to 25.5 over the last 10 days. That’s a significant loss. We gave you two units of blood in the ER to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s why I’ve been so tired. Is it from the nose and urine bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely the cause. Your INR was elevated—2.5 when you arrived, and it had been as high as 5 recently. That means your blood is too thin, which increases bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Coumadin because of my mechanical heart valve. Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held your Coumadin and aspirin for now to let your INR come down. Once you’re stable, we’ll restart them at a lower dose. Your safety comes first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the nosebleeds? They were scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ENT was consulted. They packed your nose to stop the bleeding. We’re starting you on Afrin and saline spray to keep your nasal passages moist and prevent re-bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve used Afrin before. Should I be careful not to overuse it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re prescribing it for only three days. After that, just use it if you feel a bleed starting. Overuse can cause rebound congestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the blood in my urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a urinalysis and confirmed blood, but no infection. It’s microscopic hematuria. Since your INR was high, that likely contributed. We’ve arranged an outpatient urology appointment to check further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No pain when I pee, so I wasn’t sure if it was serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good—no pain is reassuring. But we still want to rule out other causes, especially given your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. Your repeat labs show your hemoglobin is improving—up to 10.1 now. That’s a good response to the transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I’m feeling a bit stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also watching your sodium. It was low at 132, but it’s improved to 133. We held your Lasix temporarily because of the anemia and low volume state.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take it every day. Should I restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll restart it at discharge. It’s important for your heart failure, but we had to pause it briefly to help your sodium and volume stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. My back’s been bothering me—can I still take my oxycodone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can continue it as needed. Just be cautious—don’t overdo activity, especially with the nose pack in place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I reviewed your CT head from this morning. No bleeding or stroke. Your headache is likely from the anemia or dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about another stroke. I’ve had four before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your history puts you at higher risk, which is why we’re so careful with your anticoagulation. But today’s scan is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, my nose feels blocked. Is that from the packing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the packing will stay in for now. ENT will remove it tomorrow. In the meantime, use the saline spray as directed and don’t blow your nose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Vaseline? Should I keep applying that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, twice daily. It helps keep the lining moist and reduces irritation. Also, sneeze with your mouth open to reduce pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Mr. Thompson. Your hemoglobin is now 10.7, and your INR is 2.7—back in a safer range. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What changes are we making to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting Coumadin at 3 mg daily—lower than before. Aspirin continues. Lasix is back on. And we’re adding saline spray long-term, plus Afrin for three days only.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my glyburide? I check my sugar at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue glyburide. Your glucose was 77 this morning—perfect. Keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Watch for any nosebleeds or pink urine. If a nosebleed happens, spray Afrin and hold pressure for 15 minutes. Also, weigh yourself daily—call your doctor if you gain more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—PCP in one week, ENT in three days, and urology next week. We’ve coordinated everything. You’ll go home with a walker for support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel. You came in with dizziness and low blood pressure. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I woke up feeling unsteady on my feet. No spinning, just like I might fall. Also had some chest discomfort when I yawned or moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any shortness of breath, especially with activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a bit when I walk. Not bad at rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your blood pressure was low when you arrived—86 over 50—but it’s improved. We’re checking blood work to see what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heart issues before. Four strokes, a pacemaker, and a mechanical heart valve. I’m on Coumadin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see that. Your INR might be high, which could relate to bleeding risk. But your labs show your hemoglobin is very low—6.5. That’s likely why you’re dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low blood again? I had that last month with nosebleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. No active bleeding now—your stool was only faintly positive. But your red blood cell count is still low. We plan to give you three units of blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Three? Last time it was two. Did it not help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. Also, your body may be destroying red blood cells—what we call hemolysis. Your haptoglobin is very low and bilirubin is up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hemolysis? Is that from my heart valve?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. Mechanical valves can shear red cells. We’ll get a hematology consult to look into it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Your first unit of blood was given overnight. Your hemoglobin went up a little—to 7.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still low, though. Why isn’t it going up more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It suggests your body is still breaking down red cells. We’re continuing the transfusions and starting iron pills and folic acid to help your bone marrow make more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my Coumadin? Should I stop that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held it for now. Your INR was high. Once stable, we’ll restart at a lower dose. You’ll need close monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your chest X-ray. There’s mild fluid in the lungs and a slightly enlarged heart. This suggests your heart failure is worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had CHF before. I’ve been drinking more water—thought it was good for my kidney stone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be the trigger. Too much fluid can overload your heart. We’re increasing your Lasix to help remove the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? It’s usually low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered your lisinopril to 2.5 mg to avoid dropping it too much. Your Toprol stays the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your second and third blood units were given. Hemoglobin is now 8.1. Still low, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any word from hematology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They agree it’s likely mechanical hemolysis from your valve. Your Coombs test was negative, so it’s not immune-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more transfusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not for now. We’ll monitor. You’ll need follow-up with them. We’ve started omeprazole to protect your stomach, since you’re on aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is better. The Lasix is working—your leg swelling is down from 2+ to trace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel less puffy. My weight’s down too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll switch you back to your home dose of Lasix. Keep weighing yourself daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your sodium is improving—133. It was 128 on admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of the Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly. And better fluid balance. Your kidney function is also improving—creatinine down to 0.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your echocardiogram results. Your heart’s pumping at 45%—a bit low. There’s moderate pulmonary hypertension, slightly worse than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the heart failure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It means your lungs have higher pressure, which can strain the right side of the heart. We’ll keep managing your fluid and heart meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 3.9. That’s within your target range for your mechanical valve, so we’ll restart Coumadin at 2 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just 2 mg? I was taking more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to be safe. You’ll have a visiting nurse check your INR soon, and the anticoagulation clinic will guide future doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news, Mr. Thompson. You’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have appointments with your primary care doctor, a heart failure specialist, and hematology. They’ve been updated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started iron and omeprazole. Lisinopril is now 2.5 mg, and Coumadin is 2 mg daily for now. Keep taking your other heart and diabetes meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I still watch for bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Report any nosebleeds, dark stools, or unusual bruising. And call your doctor if your weight goes up more than 3 pounds in a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. A nurse will go over your discharge papers and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a final check-in. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Not dizzy, and I can walk farther without getting winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep up with your follow-ups and daily weights. We’ll see you doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—when can I drive again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. With your history of strokes and recent dizziness, it’s safest to wait until your neurologist clears you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ll ask at my next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your visiting nurse will come to check your INR in a few days. They’ll coordinate with the anticoagulation clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they adjust my Coumadin dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, based on the result. The goal is to keep it between 2.5 and 3.5 for your mechanical valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a bit nervous about the iron pills. Will they upset my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Some people get constipation or mild nausea. Take it with food. We’ve also added Colace to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. And the omeprazole—is that for my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. With aspirin and your history of ulcers, it reduces acid and protects your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge team is finalizing your transport. You’ll go home with a visiting nurse and all your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help. I’ll keep in touch with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Lee. You were brought in after a bad nosebleed, low blood pressure, and passing dark stool. We’re going to take good care of you. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m dizzy, nauseous, and my stomach hurts. The nosebleed was scary—so much blood. I thought it would never stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Your blood pressure was very low when you arrived, and your hemoglobin was down to 8.1. That explains the dizziness. We’ve given you fluids and started a blood transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been anemic before. Is this the same thing? Why isn’t the blood helping me feel better yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s anemia, but this time it’s from active bleeding—your nose and likely your stomach. The transfusion takes time. We’ll give you several units to stabilize you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had black stools for months. I thought it was just from my pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Black, tarry stools usually mean upper GI bleeding. Given your history, we’re concerned about gastritis or an ulcer. We’ll schedule an endoscopy soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they put me to sleep for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be sedated. It’s a quick procedure where we look into your stomach with a small camera. It helps us find and treat the source of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my warfarin? I’ve been on it for years because of my heart valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Your INR was 3.1—higher than your target. We’ve held warfarin and aspirin for now because of the bleeding. But we can’t stop it too long due to your mechanical valve and stroke history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what will you do instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start a heparin IV drip to keep your blood thin enough to protect your valve, but not so much that it worsens bleeding. Once you’re stable, we’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my blood pressure? It’s always been low lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family mentioned that too. It’s likely from blood loss, but we’ll monitor it. We won’t restart your blood pressure meds until we’re sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your hemoglobin dropped to 20.8% hematocrit before the transfusion. You’ve now received 3 units and are cross-matched for 4 more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I passed more black stool last night. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, which is why we’re moving up your endoscopy. We also increased your pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid and help any ulcers heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was supposed to start iron at home. Should I still do that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re delaying it until the bleeding is controlled. Starting iron too soon can irritate the stomach. We’ll restart it before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you had your endoscopy yesterday. It showed diffuse gastritis with contact bleeding in the stomach lining. No ulcers or major bleeds, but it’s likely contributing to your anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s where the blood is coming from? But what about my nose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both. The gastritis explains the GI bleeding, and your nose has been a known issue. ENT saw you and said it’s anterior bleeding. They recommended nasal saline and Vaseline to keep it moist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They gave me Afrin too, right? For only a few days?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Three days max. Overuse can make it worse. We’ve scheduled ENT follow-up to check for cauterization if it keeps happening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my heart? I felt short of breath after the transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. The extra fluid from transfusions can overload your heart, especially with diastolic dysfunction. Your chest X-ray showed mild congestion, so we gave one dose of IV furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m back on my water pill?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted your usual 20 mg furosemide daily. We also resumed low-dose metoprolol since your blood pressure is back to your baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is holding steady at 23.6%. That’s a good sign the bleeding is slowing. We’ll keep monitoring your stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had any nosebleeds since I’ve been here. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s a good sign. The nasal ointment and humidified air are helping. We’ll keep those up until discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my diabetes? I haven’t checked my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been checking them. They’ve been well-controlled. We’ve kept you on glyburide, but we lowered the dose to 5 mg daily to avoid lows, especially with poor intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the vascular congestion has improved. That means the diuretic helped. Your breathing should feel better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can lie flat now without gasping. That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll keep you on the current heart and lung meds. Your COPD is stable—just keep using your inhalers as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 1.9 yesterday, so we restarted warfarin at 2 mg nightly. We’ll check it again tomorrow. The heparin drip will stop once it’s in range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that lower than before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you were on 3 mg. We’re starting lower to avoid another high INR. Your doctor will adjust it based on your next few results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And I’m finally getting that iron, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting ferrous sulfate 324 mg daily. Take it with vitamin C for better absorption, but not on an empty stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.8—perfect. We’ve turned off the heparin. You’re fully on warfarin again at 2 mg nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I’m ready to go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We want to see one more hemoglobin check and make sure you’re eating well. You’ll need INR and CBC checks tomorrow, and the results will go to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Who do I call if I start bleeding again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your PCP or go to the ER if it’s severe. Also, watch for dizziness, chest pain, or shortness of breath. Your home health nurse will check in too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs are stable. You’ve had no melena or epistaxis. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What meds am I taking at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before, mostly. Furosemide 20 mg daily, metoprolol 12.5 mg, lisinopril 2.5 mg. But now: pantoprazole twice daily, ferrous sulfate daily, and warfarin 2 mg nightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the aspirin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll restart 81 mg daily. It’s important for your heart and stents, as long as there’s no active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your PCP in 3 days, ENT for your nose, and hematology to review your anemia. Make sure to keep all those appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I should use the nasal spray and Vaseline every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, daily. Humidify your room, especially in winter. That helps prevent nosebleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just take it easy at home. No heavy lifting. Eat iron-rich foods—spinach, red meat, beans.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, your discharge orders are ready. You’re cleared to go home with home health services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take your meds, watch for bleeding, and call if anything changes. We’ll make sure your doctors get all the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge paperwork and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your home health nurse will call tomorrow to check your INR and CBC results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be home all day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We want to make sure you’re healing well from both the stomach and nose issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve already noticed less nausea since starting the stronger stomach medicine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the pantoprazole working. Keep taking it twice a day as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll take the iron with orange juice like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent plan. That’ll help your body absorb it better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more question—should I avoid any foods with warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just keep your vitamin K intake consistent—like leafy greens. Don’t suddenly eat a lot more or less. That can affect your INR.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t have to avoid spinach altogether?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, just eat it regularly. Consistency is key.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I love my salads.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Enjoy them—just keep it steady. Same with alcohol. One drink occasionally is fine, but not more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I only have a beer on Sundays. That’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s perfectly fine. Just don’t binge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wouldn’t dream of it. I’ve learned my lesson with my health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best attitude. Keep it up, and you’ll do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really mean it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in with a nosebleed and some dark stools. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I was bending over this afternoon and suddenly my nose started bleeding a lot. It didn’t stop with pressure. And I’ve been having black, tarry stools for a few weeks now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned you’ve had this before. Are you still taking your pantoprazole for your stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Honestly, I haven’t been. I thought I was feeling better and stopped a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might be part of why this happened again. Your blood count is quite low—your hemoglobin is only 6.9. We’re going to give you two units of blood right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I’m on warfarin for my heart valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. Your INR is therapeutic at 3.4, so we won’t give vitamin K. We’ll hold the warfarin for now and restart it later when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my nose? It keeps crusting up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re using Afrin to help stop the bleeding. ENT saw you earlier and said you have nasal vestibulitis. They recommend continuing Bactroban, plus saline spray and Vaseline to keep the nose moist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. Should I start that now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll start it tonight. We also gave you an IV acid blocker to protect your stomach. You’ll switch to omeprazole by mouth soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the stomach bleed still going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re not sure yet. Your hemoglobin dropped again after the first two units, so we gave two more. A tagged red blood cell scan is scheduled tomorrow to check for active bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my breathing? I feel a bit winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid and a possible lung infection, likely from aspiration. We started antibiotics—levofloxacin and flagyl—just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. Your nosebleed has stopped, and your latest hemoglobin is up to 8.7. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The tagged RBC scan showed no active bleeding. Your melena has stopped, and your stool is now brown, though still guaiac positive. We think the gastritis flare-up has settled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was my stomach and the nose both acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Chronic gastritis, worsened by not taking your acid blocker, plus the nosebleed. Both contributed to the anemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take the omeprazole every day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. We’re switching you to oral omeprazole twice daily. It’s the best way to prevent future bleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows the lung infection is improving. The vascular congestion is a bit worse, likely from the blood transfusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed my legs are more swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have 2+ pitting edema. We gave IV Lasix yesterday and will continue with oral furosemide. We’re increasing it to twice daily for three days to help with the fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure meds? I usually take lisinopril and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held them for now because of the low blood pressure and bleeding. You’ll restart them only after talking to your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call him after I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are looking better. Hemoglobin is stable at 8.7, and your kidney function has improved. The indirect bilirubin is still a bit high, but it’s coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What was that from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s due to the mechanical heart valve and the transfusions. No signs of serious hemolysis, and it’s improving, so we’re not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my diabetes? I didn’t get my glyburide yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held it temporarily. Your sugars have been well-controlled. You’ll go back to your usual dose at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: ENT saw you this morning. They agree with the current nasal care—Bactroban, saline spray, and Vaseline. No need for cautery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep doing that every day. Anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If you have another nosebleed that doesn’t stop, or black stools again, come back right away. Also, weigh yourself daily—call if you gain more than three pounds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’re doing well. We’re discharging you today. You’re stable, no bleeding, and your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take omeprazole twice daily, continue Bactroban, and add saline spray and Vaseline for your nose. Lasix will be twice daily for three days, then back to once daily. Hold lisinopril and metoprolol until your PCP advises.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And aspirin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve stopped it for now. It increases bleeding risk. Your PCP will decide when to restart it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Follow up with your PCP, ENT, and get the labs done as scheduled. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Patel, one of your hospital doctors. You came in last night with dark stools and dizziness. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been seeing black, tarry stools for a few months now, off and on. And lately, I’ve been feeling dizzy, especially when I stand up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any nosebleeds recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had a few. They come and go. I use that nasal spray you gave me last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Your blood pressure dropped a bit in the ER, and your hemoglobin is low at 7.4 g/dL. That explains the dizziness. We’re concerned about bleeding from your stomach or nose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my heart valve medicine? I know warfarin can cause bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your INR is 2.4, which is a bit high. That means your blood is too thin. We’ll hold warfarin for now and give you a medication to reverse it if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a transfusion again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring you closely. Right now, you’re volume overloaded, so we won’t transfuse yet. We’ll treat the bleeding first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, we did a CT scan last night. It shows mild thickening in part of your small intestine, possibly mild duodenitis. But no active diverticulitis or other serious issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I’m bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we won’t know for sure until we do an endoscopy. That’s scheduled for tomorrow. We’ll look directly into your stomach and upper intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It wasn’t too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll also keep checking your blood counts and manage your heart failure. Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs, so we’ll restart your Lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My breathing’s been a little tight. Is that from the fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely. We’ll give you oxygen and diuretics to help clear it. You should feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, we did the endoscopy this morning. You have severe hemorrhagic gastritis — that means bleeding inflammation in your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is, but we’re treating it. You’re on IV pantoprazole, a strong acid reducer. We’ll switch to oral later. We also started sucralfate, which coats and protects the stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope so. Your hemoglobin has stabilized, which is a good sign. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your H. pylori test came back negative. So it’s not a bacterial infection causing the gastritis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is causing it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely, it’s from the combination of your mechanical heart valve and blood thinners. The valve causes some red blood cell damage, and warfarin increases bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m stuck with this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. We can reduce the risk. We’re restarting warfarin soon, but we’re going to stop aspirin. That should help lower your bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need aspirin for my heart, don’t I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Normally, yes. But given how often you’re bleeding, the risks outweigh the benefits. Your cardiologist agrees.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had another nosebleed last night. ENT came by and cauterized the spot with silver nitrate. It should heal in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt it start but couldn’t stop it. Should I keep using the nasal spray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue the saline spray and mupirocin ointment twice a day. Keep the inside of your nose moist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Vaseline?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can use that too, especially at night. Just don’t overdo it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is holding steady at 8.8 g/dL. That’s good progress. We’re going to start a heparin drip to bridge you back to warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that increase bleeding risk?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor your PTT closely. The dose is low and conservative. We won’t restart warfarin until we’re sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting warfarin today at a lower dose — 2.5 mg daily. Your INR will be checked daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Same time every day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, around 4 PM. We’ll make sure the nurses give it on time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no more nosebleeds, and your stools are no longer black. Your latest hemoglobin is 9.0 g/dL — that’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting close. We want to make sure your INR is stable and your heart failure is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is down to 196 pounds, and your lungs are clearer. We’ll keep you on 20 mg Lasix daily for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My dry weight is 194. Should I be worried if it goes up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If you gain more than 3 pounds in a day, call your doctor. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.1 — right in the target range. That’s great. We’ll keep monitoring, but you’re doing well on the new warfarin dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’m still on the pantoprazole and sucralfate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, both twice a day. They’ll help protect your stomach. You’ll take them at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a few days. You’ll go home with services — a nurse will check on you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ll need help with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll also start iron pills to help rebuild your blood. Take them with food to avoid stomach upset.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been high in the hospital. We’ve been using insulin. You can go back to glyburide at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I need to watch my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep using your inhalers for your COPD. You’ve needed nebs a few times, but you’re breathing well now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs look stable. Your heart function is okay — ejection fraction around 45%. We’ll hold off on restarting lisinopril and metoprolol for now due to low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can my regular doctor restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if your blood pressure stays stable. We’ll send all the details to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. You’re walking well, breathing fine, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. What do I need to remember?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your pantoprazole and sucralfate as prescribed. Continue mupirocin and saline spray for your nose. Warfarin at 2.5 mg daily. Iron twice a day with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no aspirin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We stopped it to reduce bleeding risk. Follow up with your cardiologist and gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re officially discharged. Keep monitoring your weight, watch for black stools or nosebleeds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel. You were brought in because of low blood pressure and black stools. We think you're bleeding in your stomach again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had this before. I’ve been dizzy and weak lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is quite low at 6.6. We’ve given you two units of blood already. We’ll keep monitoring you and need to find where the bleeding is coming from.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on warfarin for my heart valve. Could that be making it worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, warfarin increases bleeding risk. We’ve stopped it for now. Your INR was 2.8, which is high. We’ll restart it later when you’re more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray yesterday. It shows fluid in your lungs from heart failure. That’s likely why you’ve been short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had COPD for years. But this breathlessness is worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart isn’t pumping as efficiently as it should. We’ve started IV Lasix to help remove the extra fluid. But we have to be careful with your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped again last night. We gave you another unit of blood. We’re arranging an endoscopy to look into your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they fix the bleeding during the scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see what we find. If there’s active bleeding, they can treat it. But even if not, we need to identify the source. You’ve had many transfusions—29 since last year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds bad. Is there a chance I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery was consulted. They want to rule out cancer first with biopsies. For now, we’re focusing on stabilizing you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.1. We’re starting a heparin drip to protect your heart valve while we wait for the endoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why switch from warfarin to heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Heparin works faster and can be stopped quickly if you bleed more. It’s a bridge until we can safely restart warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound on your arms because of swelling. No clots, but the pacemaker might be affecting blood flow on the left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The swelling’s been there a while. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll monitor it. The main concern is your bleeding and heart failure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your endoscopy showed abnormal blood vessels in your stomach—angiodysplasias. No active bleeding, but they’re likely the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can they fix those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They can use a technique called APC in the future. But right now, you’re too unstable. We’ll do a capsule study to check your small intestine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The capsule study found one angiectasia in your small bowel. No active bleeding. So your stomach and small bowel are the likely sources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now? More transfusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. We’ve restarted warfarin at a lower dose with a Lovenox bridge. Goal INR is now 2.0–3.0 instead of 2.5–3.5 to reduce bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started iron, B12, and vitamin C to help your body make more blood. You’ll need these long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking iron before. Does this mean I’m still anemic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic blood loss causes iron deficiency. Even with transfusions, you need supplements to rebuild your stores.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped to 19.6. We gave you three units of blood. You also had a small episode of vomiting blood—about 125 cc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt it coming up. Was it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but your vitals stayed stable. We’re watching closely. GI decided not to intervene again for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving you to the cardiac floor. Your heart failure is improving with the diuretics, but we need to keep removing fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The Lasix made me dizzy. Are we still using it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We switched to a continuous drip to avoid big drops in blood pressure. You’re now on metolazone too to help it work better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight’s down by 3 kg. That’s good. Your breathing should be easier now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe better, yes. But I still feel tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from the anemia. As your hemoglobin stabilizes, your energy should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a colonoscopy. You have diverticulosis, but no bleeding there. So the stomach and small bowel remain the likely sources.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing can be done about the bleeding now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. But we’re setting up weekly visits at the pheresis unit for transfusions as needed. You’ll get labs before each visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting torsemide 20 mg daily instead of Lasix. It’s stronger and once-daily dosing is easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help with the fluid from transfusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You tend to retain fluid when you get blood. We may add an extra dose of torsemide with each transfusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest X-ray shows improvement in heart failure. The lung congestion is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel less puffy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to place a PICC line. It’ll make giving fluids, meds, and transfusions easier over the next few weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? Any risks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low risk. Main concern is infection, so we’ll remove it in about four weeks once you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC is in place. We’ll use it for your transfusions and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is fluctuating between 24 and 27. We’re giving blood when it drops below 25.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need transfusions forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope not. You’ll see GI soon to discuss APC therapy to treat the angiodysplasias. That could reduce or stop the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your sputum grew Staph aureus, but it’s not resistant. We’re not starting antibiotics unless you get worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing. Should I be on something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your cough is likely from heart failure and COPD. We’ll keep using inhalers and monitor. Antibiotics could upset your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your weight is stable at 78 kg. Your breathing is much better. We’re close to discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Check your weight daily. Call if it goes up more than 3 pounds. Limit fluids to 1.5 liters a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is 2.4 and hemoglobin is 27.4. You’re stable. We’re planning discharge in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole, sucralfate, and the new meds: iron, B12, vitamin C, and torsemide. Warfarin is now 2 mg daily. Check INR weekly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have weekly appointments at the pheresis unit. They’ll transfuse you if your hemoglobin is low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your cardiologist. Keep taking metoprolol and torsemide. We stopped lisinopril and furosemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing: if your hemoglobin drops below 21, go to the ER. Below 23, get two units. Below 25, get one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It will be removed in about four weeks. A nurse will help you with care at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver ultrasound showed fatty changes and a small spleen enlargement. Nothing urgent, but your PCP will monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had liver issues before. Should I change my diet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Focus on low salt and avoid alcohol. Your diabetes is well-controlled—keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home with visiting nurse services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Discharge is tomorrow. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just one—when do I see GI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Next week. They’ll discuss APC therapy to treat the stomach vessels and reduce future bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Packing up? You’re doing well. Remember: weigh daily, check INR weekly, and call if you feel worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow the plan. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check: your hemoglobin is 27.4, weight 78 kg, and you’re breathing well. All set for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to be going home. I’ll stick to the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’re cleared to go home. The nurse will go over your meds and follow-up one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call us if anything changes. See you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming: you understand when to get transfusions and how to manage your fluids and diuretics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I do. I’ll check my weight and labs and call if things go off track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Lee. You came in tonight because your blood pressure dropped during a blood transfusion. Can you tell me how you've been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt weak, but not dizzy or short of breath. They were giving me blood at the clinic when my pressure went down. I didn’t pass out or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good you stayed alert. Your hemoglobin was low at 7.7, and your INR was 2.6, which means your blood isn’t clotting as well as it should. Given your history of stomach bleeding, we’re concerned this might be another GI bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I haven’t seen black stools this time. Just dark ones. Is that still a bleed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, dark stools can still mean slow bleeding. We’ll keep monitoring your blood counts. Because of your mechanical heart valve, we have to balance bleeding risk with clotting risk. For now, we’re holding warfarin and giving you pantoprazole to protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not on my blood thinner right now? Isn’t that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a risk, but uncontrolled bleeding is more immediate. We’ll restart anticoagulation once we control the bleed. For now, we’re watching closely and may use heparin later if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your hemoglobin dropped again to 7.2 overnight, so we’re giving you another unit of blood. We’re also scheduling an endoscopy to look for the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another transfusion? How many will I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll only give what’s necessary. The goal is to stabilize you so we can do the endoscopy safely. We want to find and treat the bleeding spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid buildup in your lungs. You have heart failure, and the transfusions may be making it harder for your heart to keep up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been a bit short of breath. Is that from the fluid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re holding off on diuretics for now because your blood pressure is borderline, but we’ll restart them once we’re sure the bleeding is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we’re waiting on the heart treatment because of the stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Bleeding is the more urgent issue. Once we fix that, we can safely manage your heart failure with diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned shoulder pain yesterday. We did an X-ray, and it shows calcific tendinitis—calcium deposits in the shoulder tendon. That’s likely what’s causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? It hurts a lot when I move it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not dangerous, but it can be painful. Orthopedics recommends a steroid injection to reduce inflammation. We’ll also give you oxycodone for pain, but we’ll use it sparingly because it can affect your thinking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been a bit confused lately. Is that from the medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We checked a head CT, and there’s no bleeding or new stroke. Your confusion is likely due to the oxycodone, anemia, or both. We’ll taper the painkiller as your pain improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning your endoscopy for tomorrow. We’ll stop warfarin completely and let your INR drop to around 1.5 before the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And then you’ll fix the bleed during the scope?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. If we find angioectasias—abnormal blood vessels—we can treat them with a technique called argon-plasma coagulation to seal them off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be sedated, so you won’t feel it. Afterward, you might have a sore throat, but that’s usually the worst of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 1.5. That’s safe for the endoscopy. It’s scheduled for this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endoscopy found multiple angioectasias in your stomach, arranged in a pattern called ‘watermelon stomach.’ We used the argon-plasma coagulator to treat them all. The good news is, no active bleeding was seen after treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s fixed? No more bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve controlled it for now. These can come back, so we’ll keep you on pantoprazole and sucralfate to protect your stomach lining.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart heparin tonight, then begin warfarin tomorrow. Your cardiologist says once your INR reaches 1.6, we can stop heparin. The risk of clotting with your aortic valve is low at that level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You seemed more confused last night. We checked a head CT—no stroke or bleed. The oxycodone may be affecting you. We’re going to reduce the dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel foggy. Maybe less pain medicine would help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch to lower doses and use it only when needed. Your shoulder injection should start helping in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin has stabilized at 8.1. That’s a good sign the bleeding is controlled. We’re not giving more transfusions unless it drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my heart? I still feel a little swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you still have leg swelling. Now that the bleeding is controlled, we’re restarting your torsemide to help with fluid removal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also restarting metoprolol to help control your blood pressure and heart rate. We held it earlier because of low BP, but now it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 1.6. That’s high enough to stop heparin. We’ll continue warfarin at 3 mg nightly. The Coumadin clinic will follow your levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m back on full anticoagulation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but your target INR is now 2.0–2.5 instead of 2.0–3.0. Lower risk of bleeding, but still protective for your valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No further drops in hemoglobin. Your breathing is better, and your legs are less swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow or the day after. We want to make sure you’re stable on your medications first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are good. Hemoglobin 8.4, INR 1.6. Your heart failure is stable on torsemide. We’re finalizing your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What changes to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue pantoprazole twice daily, sucralfate four times a day, and warfarin 3 mg at bedtime. We’re starting metoprolol 25 mg daily. All other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the iron?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take ferrous sulfate daily, with vitamin C to help absorption. Follow up with GI and cardiology as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my shoulder?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue gentle movement. Follow up with orthopedics in a few weeks. The steroid shot should keep improving your pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. We’ll arrange home health services to help with monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to watch my weight, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than 3 pounds in a day, call your doctor. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And blood tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The Coumadin clinic will check your INR weekly. Your primary doctor will monitor your hemoglobin and kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more transfusions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not unless your levels drop. For now, the goal is to stay stable and prevent rebleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’re finalizing your discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—I take the sucralfate an hour before meals and the pantoprazole with food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, pantoprazole should be taken 30 minutes before meals. Sucralfate is best on an empty stomach—1 hour before or 2 hours after food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I call if I see dark stools again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, or if you feel dizzy, short of breath, or have chest pain. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you've been feeling like you're holding too much fluid lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My legs have been swelling up for about a month now, and it’s getting worse. I can’t lie flat without feeling short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re sitting up comfortably now, which makes sense. We’ll get you started on treatment right away. You’ve had this before, haven’t you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, several times. I take my meds and watch my salt, but sometimes it just builds up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your labs and did a chest X-ray. The X-ray shows fluid in your lungs and around your heart — signs of heart failure worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious, but treatable. We’re going to start you on an IV diuretic — a lasix drip — to help your body get rid of the extra fluid.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds familiar. Last time I lost a lot of weight quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We expect you’ll lose about 20 pounds of fluid over the next few days. Your kidney function looks good, so we can safely use strong diuretics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want my kidneys getting hurt.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that closely. We’ve also added metolazone, a pill that helps the lasix work better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve taken that before. It works, but I have to stay near the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s expected. We’ll keep track of your urine output to make sure you’re responding well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your chest X-ray from this morning confirms what we thought — pulmonary congestion and pleural effusions. But you’re already making more urine, which is a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been going a lot. My legs feel a little less tight already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. Your blood pressure is stable, and your breathing should keep improving as the fluid leaves your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, my blood sugar has been a bit high lately. I noticed the nurse checking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started you on a sliding scale insulin to keep your sugars between 100 and 180. Your home glyburide isn’t enough when you’re stressed like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t like insulin much, but if it helps, okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s temporary. Once you’re stable, we’ll go back to your usual diabetes meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve lost about 12 pounds of fluid so far. Your breathing is easier, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I can lie down a little now without gasping. That’s a big relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re also watching your hemoglobin. It dropped a bit to 6.9, but you’re not bleeding anywhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the last time I bled? I’m still anemic, aren’t I?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have chronic anemia from past GI bleeds. But this time, we think it’s just from dilution as your blood volume expanded. Still, we’re going to give you a unit of blood to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
