conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your medications, especially warfarin and pantoprazole. Don’t restart torsemide—that’s on hold until your primary doctor clears it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the follow-up tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—get a CBC, basic metabolic panel, and INR done in a few days. Fax the results to your primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll follow up with your primary care provider, oncology, and hepatology. Make sure to mention any black stools, vomiting, or severe belly pain right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And if I feel short of breath again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come in. But you’re much stronger now, and your heart function is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. You’re cleared for discharge. Your condition is stable, and all critical issues are addressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember—no torsemide, take pantoprazole twice daily, and keep all your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin schedule changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—now 5 mg five times a week and 7.5 mg twice a week. We updated your prescription. Your INR target remains 2.0 to 2.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the stomach cancer—how often do I need checkups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oncology will decide, but likely every few months initially. They may repeat an EGD in 6 months to ensure no recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to go. Anything else I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Signs of bleeding—black stools, dizziness, or weakness. Also, fever or severe abdominal pain. Otherwise, focus on rest and recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you leave—your weight is 82.6 kg, down from admission. That suggests you’ve lost some fluid, which is good for your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel lighter, actually.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And your oxygen level is 97% on room air—excellent. Lungs are clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can breathe so much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Keep using your inhalers for your COPD as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed the albuterol as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a sign your overall condition is improving. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my diabetes meds were held in the hospital. Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted metformin and glipizide. Watch your blood sugar, especially since your diet is back to normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually check it twice a day. I’ll keep doing that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. And if you have any questions, call the clinic. We’re here to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re confident you’ll do well. Take it easy for the next week or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. No gardening or heavy lifting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Let your body heal. And congratulations on getting through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. Really.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll also send a summary to your primary care doctor and specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want them all on the same page.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They will be. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Reyes, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you came in last night with shortness of breath, some blood in your urine, and right-sided pain. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. I’m still pretty short of breath. It started yesterday and it’s making it hard to walk even a few steps. I’m not coughing, but I feel a bit chilled now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the hematuria—when did that start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A few days ago. No pain with it, just noticed the color. I thought maybe it was from the stones I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. And your right upper quadrant pain—how’s that been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s actually getting better since the procedure on my stomach. Still there, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear it’s improving. We’ve reviewed your history—your heart function, COPD, the recent stomach cancer resection, and your mechanical valve. We’re concerned your shortness of breath might be due to pneumonia or a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pneumonia? But I don’t have a fever or cough much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not everyone does. We ordered a CT scan and chest X-ray. The CT showed multifocal pneumonia in both lungs and a small fluid collection on the right side—pleural effusion. That could be contributing to your breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious? I just got out of the hospital a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because you’ve been hospitalized recently, we have to be cautious about more resistant infections. Your white blood cell count is high, so we’re starting you on strong antibiotics—vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and doxycycline—for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on those the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess. We also swabbed for MRSA—results back tomorrow. If it’s negative and you improve, we can switch to oral antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. What about my breathing treatments? I usually use my inhalers at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on duonebs—albuterol and ipratropium—every six hours. You can still use your albuterol as needed. We’re also adding a short course of steroids—prednisone—for five days to help with COPD flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids? My sugar runs high sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we know. Your A1c is 6.8%. We’ve held your metformin and glipizide for now and are monitoring your sugars closely. We’ll restart them when you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I’ve been taking my torsemide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your BNP is quite high—3330—higher than last admission. That suggests your heart is under strain. We gave you IV furosemide to help remove fluid. Your leg swelling is already improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll go back to torsemide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. At discharge, we’ll have you continue torsemide, limit fluids to two liters a day, and keep sodium under 2 grams. We’ll also ask you to check your weight daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the blood in my urine? Should I see urology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT showed your kidney stones are still there but not blocking anything. No hydronephrosis. The bleeding may be from the stones or your INR being high. We held your warfarin temporarily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My INR was high? I’ve been on warfarin for my valve for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your INR was supratherapeutic. Infections and poor intake can affect it. We’ve resumed warfarin with a lower dose. Goal is 2.0 to 2.5. You’ll need close monitoring with your PCP after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up. What about my stomach pain? It’s better, but still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT didn’t show any new issues. Cholelithiasis is there, but no signs of cholecystitis. We’ll keep you on pantoprazole and monitor. Continue your oncology follow-up for the gastric cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. You’re looking better. Your breathing has improved, and your white count is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel a bit better. Less short of breath. Any news on the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: MRSA screen was negative, so we’re switching you from IV vancomycin and ceftriaxone to oral Augmentin and doxycycline. You’ll finish a 10-day course at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I get my nebulizer at home? I think it helps more than the inhaler.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re arranging a home nebulizer for you. Your PCP can evaluate if adding tiotropium would help long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What about my pain meds? I’ve been using oxycodone for my back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing oxycodone as needed. We’ll also send acetaminophen for the right-sided discomfort. Avoid NSAIDs due to your stomach history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, your labs today look good. White count is down to 8.2, and your hemoglobin is stable at 8.1. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the Augmentin and doxycycline for pneumonia, prednisone for two more days, and your regular heart and diabetes meds. Use the nebulizer as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the warfarin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back to your usual schedule—5 mg five times a week, 7.5 mg twice a week. Your INR was 2.0 this morning—perfect. Follow up with your doctor in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And urology for the blood in urine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we recommend outpatient urology follow-up. The stones aren’t blocking, but they could be causing the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach? Should I still get those EGDs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Continue your oncology and GI follow-up for surveillance. The resection was successful, but we need to monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll need a repeat chest X-ray in six weeks to make sure the pneumonia and effusion have cleared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your breathing is much better, labs are stable, and you’re walking well with your walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. Just want to make sure I understand everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Take your antibiotics for 10 days, finish the prednisone, keep up with torsemide, fluid and salt limits, and daily weights. Restart all your usual meds except we’ll adjust warfarin as discussed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-ups?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—PCP in one week for INR, urology for hematuria, oncology/GI for stomach cancer, and repeat chest X-ray in six weeks. Call if you have fever, worsening breathing, or chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my blood sugar was high. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was elevated due to infection and steroids. Now that you’re on oral meds again, it should stabilize. Monitor at home and report any consistent highs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my liver? I know I have cirrhosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver looks stable—no ascites or varices on CT. Continue avoiding alcohol and follow up with hepatology if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? EF is still low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, EF 35–40%. That’s why we’re strict on fluids and sodium. Keep taking your metoprolol and aspirin. Report any sudden weight gain or worsening fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over your prescriptions and discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll review everything with her.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Take care, Mr. Thompson.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your pain on the right side. If it worsens or you develop fever, call your doctor. Could be gallbladder, though it’s not inflamed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And remember—no over-the-counter meds without checking with your doctor, especially with your warfarin and stomach history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, I'm Dr. Lee. You came in tonight because of dark, black stools. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I noticed two days ago my bowel movements turned black. I didn’t feel sick, no pain or dizziness, but it worried me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called melena, and it usually means there’s bleeding in the upper part of your digestive tract. Given your history of stomach cancer and recent biopsy, that’s likely the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… so the cancer came back? I thought they removed it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The biopsy after your procedure showed some residual cancer cells. That doesn’t mean it’s spread, but it does mean we need to talk with oncology about next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I missed my appointment with them last week. My daughter was supposed to help me get there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve spoken with your daughter. She’ll help you keep your follow-up appointments. For now, we’re focused on stopping the bleeding and getting your blood levels up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. My blood count was low, right? I remember them saying that in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin was 7.0, which is quite low. We’re giving you one unit of blood to help with that. You should start feeling stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Coumadin? I take that for my heart valve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR was 4.0, which is too high. That means your blood is too thin, increasing your risk of bleeding. We’ve held your warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t that make my heart valve dangerous? I’ve had strokes before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’re starting a short-acting blood thinner called heparin to protect your valve while your INR comes down. Once it’s safer, we’ll restart warfarin at a lower dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my stomach? Is it still bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you an IV medication called pantoprazole to reduce stomach acid and help the area heal. The GI team doesn’t think you need another scope right now since your vital signs are stable and no new blood is showing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I don’t want another scope if I don’t need it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Thompson. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, doctor. I feel okay. Tired, but no more black stools.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your labs show your hemoglobin went up to 7.8 after the transfusion. We also checked your iron levels — they’re very low, so we’ll give you an IV iron supplement called ferric gluconate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already take iron pills. Why do I need IV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your body isn’t absorbing enough from the pills, and with the recent bleeding, we need to replenish your iron faster. We’ll keep the oral iron too, but we’re cautious about increasing the dose because it can cause constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hate being constipated. I’ll stick with what I have.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR dropped to 2.8 today. Still a bit high, but coming down. We’ll continue holding warfarin and keep you on heparin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any chance I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need your INR in the safe range and your hemoglobin stable. We also need to make sure there’s no more bleeding. This will take a few more days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been thinking — what happens with the stomach cancer? Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted a surgeon. You may need a partial gastrectomy — removing part of your stomach — but that depends on what the oncologist recommends. You’ll have an outpatient appointment to discuss options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds serious. Am I strong enough for surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re at high risk because of your heart and liver disease, but not impossible. We did a cardiac evaluation while you’re here. You don’t need more heart tests before surgery, but your team will weigh the risks carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your INR is now 2.4, and your hemoglobin is stable at 8.1. We’re going to restart warfarin today at a lower dose: 5 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the heparin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it for another day to overlap with warfarin, then stop it once we’re sure the warfarin is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My feet are a little swollen. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a small amount of fluid buildup. You have heart failure, and we held your diuretic early on because of the bleeding. We’re restarting torsemide today — it should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that pill. It makes me go to the bathroom a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s how it removes extra fluid. We’ll start at 30 mg and may increase it if needed. Your blood pressure is a bit low, so we’re being cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.2 — perfect. We’ve stopped the heparin. You’re back on warfarin alone. We’ll check it again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. So I’m healing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. No signs of active bleeding, your hemoglobin is holding at 8.0, and you’re feeling well. We’re planning for discharge in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, what about my diabetes? I haven’t taken my pills since I got here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been managing your blood sugar with insulin shots while you’re in the hospital. Your glucose was high this morning — 203 — so we’ll keep an eye on it. You’ll go back to your oral meds at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it doesn’t stay high. My dad had bad diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your labs look stable. We’re scheduling your discharge for tomorrow, if all goes well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I want to get home. But I’m nervous about the bleeding coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on pantoprazole 40 mg daily to protect your stomach. Take it for four weeks. If you see black stools, blood in vomit, or feel dizzy, go to the ER right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to ask — what about my heart meds? I’m not on an ACE inhibitor like some people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re allergic to lisinopril, so we can’t use that. But your primary doctor should consider other options like spironolactone or a combo of hydralazine and isosorbide to help your heart. We’ve noted that in your records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, you’re cleared for discharge tomorrow. Your hemoglobin is 8.0, INR is 2.2, and you’ve had no further bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your medications as listed. Especially warfarin — 5 mg five days a week, 7.5 mg two days. Get your INR checked in a week. And follow up with your PCP, cardiologist, and oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help getting to appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be going home with visiting nurse services. They’ll help with meds, check your weight, and make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one more thing — my liver. I know I have cirrhosis. Is that getting worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver looks stable — no ascites or big varices on the CT. But you should avoid alcohol and follow up with hepatology. NASH and amiodarone both affect your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check — all labs are good. You’re scheduled to leave tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day. Your discharge papers are ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my walker? I feel a bit unsteady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you should use your walker for support. The nurse will review safety tips. And wear those pneumoboots if your legs swell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel confused again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen, especially with age and medical issues. If it gets worse or you’re not acting like yourself, call your doctor or go to the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, just before I go — will I need chemo for the cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s for the oncologist to decide. It depends on the final staging. But given it’s early stage, surgery might be enough. Don’t worry — your team will guide you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep that appointment. My daughter’s driving me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good plan. Stay on your pantoprazole, take your warfarin, and monitor for any bleeding. You’ve done well here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. You’re discharged. Take it easy, and we’ll be in touch through your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate everything.
